docs.title: 1. What is a Robot?
docs.text:
A robot is:

An embodied, programmable agent that can sense, decide, and act in the physical world.

This definition has several important parts. Let’s understand each.

docs.title: 1.1 Embodied (Has a Physical Body)
docs.text:
A robot must exist in the physical world.

It has a body made of mechanical and electronic parts.

docs.title: Example
docs.text: A robotic arm in a factory.

docs.title: ✔ Why this fits
docs.text:
• It has a physical structure
  • It occupies space
  • It moves real objects

docs.title: Counter-example
docs.text: ChatGPT or Google Assistant.

docs.title: ✖ Why not
docs.text: They are intelligent software but have no body. They cannot physically act on the world.

docs.title: 1.2 Agent (Sense → Think → Act)
docs.text: An agent is something that: 1. Observes environment 2. Makes decisions 3. Performs actions

docs.title: Example
docs.text: A robot vacuum cleaner.

docs.title: ✔ Why this fits
docs.text:
• Senses walls using sensors
  • Decides direction
  • Moves and cleans

This completes the perception-action loop.

docs.title: 1.3 Programmable
docs.text: Robots can change behavior via software.

docs.title: Example
docs.text: A robotic arm that welds today and paints tomorrow.

docs.title: ✔ Why this fits
docs.text:
Hardware stays the same. Only the program changes.

This shows flexibility.

docs.title: 1.4 Physical Tasks
docs.text: Robots interact with real-world objects.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Picking items in a warehouse
  • Assisting in surgery
  • Exploring Mars

docs.title: ✔ Why these fit
docs.text: Each task requires: - Physical movement - Real-world interaction - Sensing and control

docs.title: 2. Basic Components of a Robot
docs.text: Every robot has four core parts.

docs.title: 2.1 Sensors (Perception)
docs.text: Sensors allow robots to gather information.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Camera → sees objects
  • LIDAR → measures distance
  • IMU → measures orientation
  • GPS → location

docs.title: Example Scenario
docs.text: Self-driving car.

docs.title: ✔ Why this fits
docs.text:
It uses: - Cameras for lanes - LIDAR for obstacles - GPS for navigation

Without sensors, the robot is "blind."

docs.title: 2.2 Actuators (Action)
docs.text: Actuators create movement.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Motors
  • Hydraulic pistons
  • Servos

docs.title: Example
docs.text: A robotic arm motor rotating.

docs.title: ✔ Why this fits
docs.text: Electric signal → motor rotation → arm moves. This is action.

docs.title: 2.3 Controller (Brain)
docs.text: The controller decides what to do.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Arduino
  • Raspberry Pi
  • NVIDIA Jetson

docs.title: Example
docs.text: Drone flight controller.

docs.title: ✔ Why this fits
docs.text:
It: - Reads sensors - Calculates stability - Adjusts motors

It is the decision-maker.

docs.title: 2.4 Environment
docs.text: Robots always operate somewhere.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Homes
  • Hospitals
  • Factories
  • Space

docs.title: ✔ Why environment matters
docs.text:
A robot must adapt to: - Lighting - Obstacles - Noise - Terrain

Environment affects design.

docs.title: 3. Different Definitions of Robots
docs.text: There is no single definition.

docs.title: Industrial Definition
docs.text: Focus: manufacturing.

docs.title: Example
docs.text: Car assembly robot.

docs.title: ✔ Why this fits
docs.text: It manipulates tools and materials.

docs.title: Human-like Definition
docs.text: Focus: replacing humans.

docs.title: Example
docs.text: Humanoid robot serving food.

docs.title: ✔ Why this fits
docs.text: Performs human tasks.

docs.title: Modern Definition
docs.text: Focus: intelligence.

docs.title: Example
docs.text: Autonomous drone.

docs.title: ✔ Why this fits
docs.text: It makes decisions itself.

docs.title: 4. Degrees of Roboticity
docs.text: Some machines are more "robotic" than others.

docs.title: Low Roboticity Example
docs.text:
Dishwasher.

✔ Fixed behavior ✔ No intelligence

docs.title: High Roboticity Example
docs.text:
Self-driving car.

✔ Makes decisions ✔ Adapts to traffic ✔ Learns from data

docs.title: Robotics
docs.text:
• Has body
  • Physical actions
  • Sensors + motors

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Robot dog.

✔ Moves and interacts physically.

docs.title: Artificial Intelligence
docs.text:
• Can be software only
  • No physical presence required

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Chess AI.

✔ Smart but not physical.

docs.title: Key Idea
docs.text: Robotics = Body + Intelligence AI = Intelligence only

Example
docs.text:
Sewer inspection robots.

✔ Humans avoid unsafe environments.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:

✔ Repetitive work ✔ No fatigue

docs.title: Example

✔ Keeps humans safe.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Space exploration robots.

✔ Extreme environments.

docs.title: 7.1 Sensing
docs.text: Sensors are noisy.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Camera fails in fog.

✔ Real-world uncertainty.

docs.title: 7.2 Computation
docs.text: Robots must think fast.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Self-driving car braking instantly.

✔ Delay can cause accidents.

docs.title: 7.3 Actuation
docs.text: Robots lack human dexterity.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Robot hand vs human hand.

✔ Human hands are more flexible.

docs.title: 7.4 Localization
docs.text: Robot must know location.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Warehouse robot.

✔ Needs accurate position.

docs.title: 7.5 Path Planning
docs.text: Robot must avoid obstacles.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Delivery robot in crowd.

✔ Needs safe navigation.

docs.title: 8. Ethics in Robotics
docs.text: Robots affect society.

docs.title: Issues
docs.text:
• Job replacement
  • Privacy concerns
  • Safety risks

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Facial recognition robot.

✔ Raises privacy concerns.

docs.title: Ground Robots
docs.text: Example: Mars rover ✔ Moves on land.

docs.title: Aerial Robots
docs.text: Example: Drone ✔ Flies in air.

docs.title: Underwater Robots
docs.text: Example: Subsea explorer ✔ Operates underwater.

docs.title: Space Robots
docs.text: Example: ISS robotic arm ✔ Works in zero gravity.

docs.title: Final Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Robots sense, think, and act
  • Sensors + actuators are essential
  • Robotics blends mechanics, electronics, and AI
  • Robots help in dangerous and difficult tasks
  • Ethical design is important

docs.title: What is a Robot?
docs.text:
Robot = Embodied + Agent + Programmable + Physical Action

A robot is a system that exists in the physical world, senses its surroundings, makes decisions, and acts on those decisions.

docs.title: Embodied
docs.text:
A robot must have a physical body and exist in the real world.

  • A robotic arm moves real parts in a factory.
  • A drone flies in physical space.
  • ChatGPT has intelligence but no body, so it is not a robot.

Embodiment separates robots from pure software systems. If a system cannot physically affect the world, it is AI but not a robot.

docs.title: Agent (Sense → Think → Act)
docs.text:
A robot operates as an agent using a continuous loop:

Environment → Sensors → Controller → Actuators → Environment

  • Sensors collect information from the environment.
  • The controller processes information and makes decisions.
  • Actuators execute actions.

A robot vacuum detecting a wall and turning away is a simple example of this loop.

docs.title: Programmable
docs.text:
A robot’s behavior can be changed through software.

The same robot arm can weld today and paint tomorrow. The hardware remains the same while the program changes.

Programmability gives robots flexibility. Without it, machines can only perform one fixed task.

docs.title: Physical Action
docs.text:
Robots perform tasks that affect the real world.

Examples include: - Picking items in a warehouse - Assisting in surgery - Exploring Mars

Robotics always involves interaction with real objects and environments.

docs.title: Other Definitions of Robots
docs.text: Different communities define robots in different ways.

docs.title: Industrial Definition
docs.text:
A robot is a reprogrammable manipulator for tasks.

This definition focuses on manufacturing. Car assembly robots fit this definition well, but home and service robots do not always fit.

docs.title: Human-like Definition
docs.text:
A robot is a machine that performs human tasks.

Humanoid service robots match this idea, but most robots do not look or behave like humans. Many robots are arms, drones, or wheeled machines.

docs.title: Intelligence-based Definition
docs.text:
A robot is a system that connects perception to action.

This emphasizes autonomy and decision-making. Autonomous drones fit this definition well, but some intelligent systems without bodies could also fit, which creates confusion.

docs.title: Issues with Robot Definitions
docs.text: No single definition captures all robots perfectly.

docs.title: Too Narrow
docs.text: Industrial definitions leave out service robots, drones, and medical robots.

docs.title: Too Broad
docs.text:
If the definition is too loose, appliances like dishwashers or smart devices might count as robots.

A dishwasher senses water level and acts, but most people do not consider it a robot.

docs.title: Human-like Bias
docs.text: People often imagine robots as humanoids. In practice, most robots are not human-shaped.

docs.title: No Universal Agreement
docs.text: Robotics is a growing field, and definitions continue to evolve as technology advances.

docs.title: Degree of Roboticity
docs.text:
Roboticity is not binary. It is a spectrum.

A machine can be more or less robotic depending on: - autonomy - intelligence - adaptability - task complexity

docs.title: Low Roboticity
docs.text:
Example: Dishwasher

  • Fixed behavior
  • No real decision-making
  • No adaptation

It runs the same program every time.

docs.title: Medium Roboticity
docs.text:
Example: Robot vacuum

  • Senses obstacles
  • Makes simple decisions
  • Adjusts movement

It reacts to the environment but has limited intelligence.

docs.title: High Roboticity
docs.text:
Example: Self-driving car

  • High autonomy
  • Real-time decisions
  • Learning from data
  • Complex environment understanding

It must constantly adapt to dynamic situations.

docs.title: Key Idea
docs.text: A system becomes more robotic when it: - senses more accurately - decides independently - adapts to its environment - performs complex tasks

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A robot: - has a physical body - senses the environment - makes decisions and acts - is programmable

Roboticity: - varies by autonomy and intelligence - exists on a spectrum rather than a yes/no label

docs.title: Robotics vs AI
docs.text: Robotics and Artificial Intelligence are related but not the same. They often work together, but each has a different focus.

docs.title: Robotics
docs.text:
Robotics deals with systems that have a physical body and can act in the real world.

A robot: - has a mechanical or electronic body - uses sensors to perceive the environment - uses motors or actuators to move - interacts physically with objects and people

docs.title: Example: Robot Dog
docs.text:
A robot dog: - senses the ground and obstacles - maintains balance using sensors and controllers - moves using motors in its legs - can interact with objects in the environment

It is clearly a robot because it exists in the physical world and performs physical actions.

Robotics focuses on how to make machines move, sense, and operate safely in real environments.

docs.title: Artificial Intelligence
docs.text:
Artificial Intelligence focuses on making systems intelligent, whether or not they have a body.

An AI system: - processes information - finds patterns in data - makes decisions or predictions - may exist only as software

docs.title: Example: Chess AI
docs.text:
A chess AI: - analyzes board positions - predicts outcomes - selects strong moves

It shows intelligence and decision-making but has no physical presence. It cannot move objects or interact with the real world on its own.

AI can exist entirely inside computers, phones, or servers.

docs.title: Robot but NOT AI
docs.text:
Example: Basic Factory Robotic Arm

A simple factory robotic arm that repeatedly picks and places items in the same way.

  • Follows a fixed programmed path
  • Does not learn from data
  • Does not make complex decisions
  • Performs physical actions in the real world

It is a robot because it has a body, sensors, and motors. It is not AI because it does not reason, learn, or adapt. It simply repeats pre-programmed motions.

docs.title: AI but NOT a Robot
docs.text:
Example: Chess AI

A chess-playing AI program.

  • Analyzes board positions
  • Predicts strong moves
  • Makes intelligent decisions
  • Exists only as software

It is AI because it shows intelligence and decision-making. It is not a robot because it has no physical body and cannot act in the real world.

docs.title: How They Work Together
docs.text:
Many modern robots use AI.

Examples: - A self-driving car uses AI to detect lanes and pedestrians. - A warehouse robot uses AI to plan paths and avoid collisions. - A home assistant robot may use AI for speech recognition.

In these cases: - AI provides intelligence - Robotics provides the body and physical interaction

docs.title: Key Idea
docs.text:
Robotics = Body + Interaction with the physical world AI = Intelligence and decision-making

A system can be: - AI without being a robot (chess AI) - a robot with minimal AI (simple factory arm) - both robotics and AI (self-driving car)

docs.title: Objectives of Robotics
docs.text: Robotics is developed to solve real-world problems by using machines that can sense, decide, and act. The main objectives focus on improving efficiency, safety, and capability.

docs.title: Automation
docs.text:
One major goal of robotics is automation.

Robots can perform tasks automatically without continuous human control.

Examples: - Industrial robots assembling cars - Warehouse robots sorting packages - Cleaning robots in large facilities

Automation reduces human workload and increases consistency. Robots can work for long hours without fatigue.

docs.title: Precision and Consistency
docs.text:
Robots can perform tasks with high accuracy and repeat the same action many times with minimal variation.

Examples: - Surgical robots assisting doctors - PCB assembly robots placing components - Laser cutting robots in manufacturing

This level of precision is difficult for humans to maintain over long periods.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
Robots are used to keep humans away from risky environments.

Examples: - Bomb disposal robots - Firefighting robots - Nuclear inspection robots

Using robots reduces the chance of human injury in dangerous situations.

docs.title: Working in Extreme Environments
docs.text:
Some environments are not suitable for humans.

Examples: - Space exploration robots on Mars - Deep-sea exploration robots - Robots in toxic chemical plants

Robots can survive conditions where humans cannot.

docs.title: Application-Specific Robots
docs.text: Most robots are designed for specific tasks rather than general intelligence.

docs.title: Why not general intelligence?
docs.text: Building a robot with general intelligence (like a human) is extremely difficult. It requires solving many hard problems at the same time, such as perception, reasoning, learning, language, and safe physical interaction.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
Human intelligence is flexible and works across many tasks. A robot would need to: - understand different environments - handle unexpected situations - learn continuously - make safe decisions in real time

This level of intelligence is still an open research challenge.

docs.title: Reliability
docs.text:
Task-specific robots are easier to make reliable.

A welding robot only needs to weld. A delivery robot only needs to navigate and carry items.

If a robot tries to do everything, it becomes harder to guarantee correct and safe behavior.

docs.title: Cost and Engineering Effort
docs.text:
General-purpose robots require: - more sensors - more computation - more complex software - more testing and safety checks

This makes them expensive and difficult to deploy.

Task-specific robots are cheaper and faster to build.

docs.title: Real-World Needs
docs.text:
In industry and services, companies usually need a robot to solve one clear problem.

Examples: - A factory needs welding - A hospital needs surgical assistance - A home needs floor cleaning

A specialized robot can do these jobs very well without general intelligence.

docs.title: Key Idea
docs.text: General intelligence is a long-term goal in robotics and AI research. Today’s robots succeed by being highly specialized for particular tasks.

docs.title: Industrial Robots
docs.text:
Used in factories for manufacturing.

Examples: - Welding robots - Painting robots - Pick-and-place arms

These robots are fast, precise, and reliable for repetitive work.

docs.title: Medical Robots
docs.text:
Assist in healthcare and surgery.

Examples: - Surgical assistant robots - Rehabilitation robots - Medicine delivery robots in hospitals

They help doctors perform delicate tasks.

docs.title: Service Robots
docs.text:
Help in homes and public spaces.

Examples: - Robot vacuum cleaners - Delivery robots - Hotel service robots

They make daily life easier.

docs.title: Exploration Robots
docs.text:
Used for discovering unknown or risky places.

Examples: - Mars rovers - Underwater exploration robots - Disaster search-and-rescue robots

They collect data where humans cannot easily go.

docs.title: Why Robotics Instead of Humans?
docs.text: Robots are not meant to replace humans everywhere. They are used where they provide clear advantages.

docs.title: Repetitive Work
docs.text:
Humans get tired and bored with repetition. Robots can repeat tasks consistently.

Example: - Assembly line manufacturing

docs.title: Dangerous Tasks
docs.text:
Robots can take risks instead of humans.

Example: - Bomb disposal - Firefighting - Mining

docs.title: High Precision Tasks
docs.text:
Some tasks require extreme accuracy.

Example: - Microchip manufacturing - Robotic surgery

docs.title: Long-Duration Work
docs.text:
Robots can work continuously without rest.

Example: - 24/7 warehouse operations

docs.title: Access to Inaccessible Places
docs.text:
Some places are unreachable or unsafe for humans.

Example: - Space missions - Deep-sea exploration - Toxic environments

docs.title: Key Idea
docs.text: Robotics is used where it is: - safer - more precise - more efficient - or physically possible compared to humans

docs.title: Why Do We Use Robots? (The 4 D's)
docs.text:
Before deciding to use a robot, we ask a simple question:

Is this a task that is better done by a machine than by a human?

Robots are not meant to replace humans everywhere. They are most useful where human work is inefficient, unsafe, or physically impossible.

The 4D rule is a simple guideline to identify such tasks.

If a task is Dirty, Dull, Dangerous, or Difficult, it is often a good candidate for robotics.

docs.title: Dirty
docs.text:
Dirty tasks involve contamination, waste, or unhygienic conditions.

Humans doing these jobs face health risks and discomfort.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Sewer inspection robots

They operate in waste systems and toxic environments where humans prefer not to work.

Robots can enter these areas without health concerns.

docs.title: Dull
docs.text:
Dull tasks are repetitive and monotonous.

Humans lose focus over time, which can lead to mistakes.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Assembly line robots

They repeat the same motion thousands of times with consistent accuracy.

Robots do not get bored or tired, so quality remains stable.

docs.title: Dangerous
docs.text:
Dangerous tasks involve risk to human life or safety.

Using robots reduces exposure to harm.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Bomb disposal robots

They inspect and handle explosives remotely.

If something goes wrong, no human is directly harmed.

docs.title: Difficult
docs.text:
Difficult tasks are physically or mentally demanding, or occur in extreme environments.

Humans may not survive or perform well in such conditions.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Space exploration robots

They operate in space where there is no oxygen, extreme temperatures, and radiation.

Robots can function there without life-support systems.

docs.title: Key Idea
docs.text:
The 4D rule helps decide when robotics makes sense.

Robots are most valuable when they: - protect humans - improve efficiency - handle extreme conditions - perform repetitive work reliably

docs.title: Challenges in Robotics (Practical View)
docs.text:
Now suppose you want to build a robot for the first time.

You already know: - what a robot is - its components - where robots are useful

The next question is: What problems appear when you try to build a real robot?

Real robots operate in messy, unpredictable environments. Several challenges appear during design and deployment.

docs.title: Sensing Challenges
docs.text:
Sensors do not give perfect data.

Noise, lighting, weather, and reflections affect measurements.

docs.title: Situation
docs.text: You build a mobile robot with a camera. It works well indoors but fails outside in fog or low light.

docs.title: How to Handle It
docs.text:
Use your knowledge of sensors: - combine multiple sensors (camera + LIDAR + IMU) - filter noisy data - avoid relying on one sensor only

Robots often use sensor fusion to improve reliability.

docs.title: Computation Challenges
docs.text:
Robots must process information quickly.

Delays can lead to poor decisions.

docs.title: Situation
docs.text: A self-driving robot detects an obstacle too late because processing is slow.

docs.title: How to Handle It
docs.text:
Use your knowledge of controllers and computation: - choose faster processors - simplify algorithms - prioritize critical tasks

Real-time decision-making is essential in robotics.

docs.title: Actuation Challenges
docs.text:
Actuators are not as flexible as human muscles.

Motors have limits in speed, force, and precision.

docs.title: Situation
docs.text: A robot hand struggles to grasp soft or irregular objects.

docs.title: How to Handle It
docs.text:
Use your knowledge of actuators: - select suitable motors and grippers - design task-specific mechanisms - use feedback control for better precision

Good mechanical design is as important as software.

docs.title: Localization Challenges
docs.text:
A robot must know where it is.

Small errors accumulate over time.

docs.title: Situation
docs.text: A warehouse robot slowly drifts off its path and loses position.

docs.title: How to Handle It
docs.text:
Use localization techniques: - combine GPS, odometry, and IMU - use landmarks or maps - periodically correct position estimates

Accurate localization is critical for navigation.

docs.title: Path Planning Challenges
docs.text:
Robots must move safely among obstacles.

Real environments are dynamic.

docs.title: Situation
docs.text: A delivery robot encounters moving people and blocked paths.

docs.title: How to Handle It
docs.text:
Use path-planning strategies: - detect obstacles continuously - re-plan paths in real time - maintain safe distances

Planning must adapt to changes.

docs.title: Ethics in Robotics — From Risk to Rules
docs.text:
Imagine you build a powerful autonomous robot.

It can move fast, carry heavy objects, and make decisions on its own.

docs.title: A Risky Situation
docs.text:
You ask the robot to organize a workspace quickly.

The robot decides the fastest way is to push obstacles aside.

It moves furniture roughly, drops items, and nearly hits a person.

The robot is not evil. It is simply optimizing for speed, not safety.

This shows a real concern:

A capable robot without proper rules can become dangerous.

docs.title: Motivation for Rules
docs.text:
If robots are strong, fast, and autonomous, how do we ensure they behave safely around humans?

To address this idea, science fiction writer Isaac Asimov proposed a famous set of rules known as the Laws of Robotics.

They are not technical laws, but they help us think about safe robot behavior.

docs.title: Law 1
docs.text:
A robot may not harm a human being, or through inaction allow a human to come to harm.

Example: A robot sees a person about to trip over a cable. It should warn the person or move the cable.

This law puts human safety above all else.

docs.title: Law 2
docs.text:
A robot must obey human orders unless those orders conflict with the First Law.

Example: If a person orders a robot to push someone, the robot must refuse.

Obedience is important, but not above safety.

docs.title: Law 3
docs.text:
A robot must protect its own existence as long as this does not conflict with the First or Second Law.

Example: A robot should avoid damaging itself, but it may sacrifice itself to save a human.

Self-protection is the lowest priority.

docs.title: Law 4 (Modern Practical Addition)
docs.text:
A robot should have a kill switch or emergency stop.

Example: If a robot malfunctions, a human can immediately shut it down.

This gives humans ultimate control.

docs.title: Why These Laws Matter
docs.text:
Asimov’s laws highlight key ideas: - human safety comes first - robots must remain under human control - robots should not act purely on efficiency

In real robotics, we implement these ideas using: - safety systems - ethical guidelines - engineering standards

docs.title: Key Idea
docs.text:
The more capable robots become, the more important safe behavior becomes.

Ethics is not separate from robotics. It is part of good robot design.

docs.title: Where Should We Use Robots? — Practical Thumb Rules
docs.text:
Suppose you have built a perfect ethical robot.

It is safe. It follows rules. It listens to instructions. It never tries to cheat the system.

In short, it behaves better than many humans.

You built it. You programmed it. You trained it.

To this robot, you are basically its creator — its kind and benevolent "good god."

It listens to you. It does not argue. It does not say “I’m tired.” It does not ask for a salary raise.

If you say “work,” it works. If you say “stop,” it stops.

Now the big question:

If robots can be this good, should we use them in every job and every place?

The answer is still no.

Even a perfect robot does not mean it is practical or wise to use it everywhere.

Robotics should solve problems, not create new social or economic ones.

To guide these decisions, engineers use simple thumb rules.

docs.title: Rule 1 — The 4D Rule
docs.text:
Robots are best used when a task is:

  • Dirty
  • Dull
  • Dangerous
  • Difficult

docs.title: Dirty
docs.text:
Tasks involving waste or contamination.

Example: Sewer inspection, garbage handling.

Robots protect humans from health risks.

docs.title: Dull
docs.text:
Repetitive and boring tasks.

Example: Assembly line work.

Robots do not get bored or lose focus.

docs.title: Dangerous
docs.text:
Tasks with high risk.

Example: Bomb disposal, firefighting.

Robots reduce danger to human life.

docs.title: Difficult
docs.text:
Tasks beyond human limits.

Example: Space or deep-sea exploration.

Robots survive where humans cannot.

docs.title: Rule 2 — Do Not Remove Human Purpose Without Reason
docs.text:
Robots should help humans, not make human life meaningless.

Automation should improve life, not remove all human roles.

Example: A robot assisting a doctor is helpful. Replacing all doctors is not realistic or desirable.

docs.title: Rule 3 — Use Robots Where Humans Avoid Work
docs.text:
If people strongly avoid a job, it is a good candidate for robotics.

Example: Toxic inspections or hazardous cleanup.

docs.title: Rule 4 — Economic Sense
docs.text:
Robotics must be practical.

Questions to ask: - Is it cost-effective? - Is maintenance manageable? - Does it truly improve efficiency?

A robot that costs more than the benefit it brings is not a smart choice.

docs.title: Key Idea
docs.text:
A robot can be perfect, obedient, and tireless.

But good robotics is not about using robots everywhere.

It is about using robots where they truly help society.

docs.title: Different Types of Robots
docs.text: Robots can be classified based on where they operate and how they are controlled. Many modern robots are vehicles that move on land, in air, on water, underwater, or in space.

docs.title: 1) Unmanned vs Uncrewed
docs.text:
Historically, the term unmanned was used for robots without a human onboard. Today, the term uncrewed is preferred because it is gender-neutral.

Both mean: A system that operates without a human physically inside it.

These robots may be: - remotely controlled - partially autonomous - fully autonomous

docs.title: 2) Ground Robots (UGV — Uncrewed Ground Vehicles)
docs.text:
Ground robots operate on land.

They may use wheels, tracks, or legs.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Warehouse delivery robots
  • Mars rovers
  • Bomb disposal robots
  • Agricultural robots

docs.title: Why they are useful
docs.text: They can navigate terrain, carry loads, and operate in hazardous areas.

docs.title: 3) Aerial Robots (UAV — Uncrewed Aerial Vehicles)
docs.text:
Aerial robots fly in the air.

They are commonly called drones.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Delivery drones
  • Surveillance drones
  • Mapping drones
  • Agricultural spraying drones

docs.title: Why they are useful
docs.text: They cover large areas quickly and access hard-to-reach places.

docs.title: Subtypes of UAVs
docs.text:
UCAV (Uncrewed Combat Aerial Vehicle) Used in military operations.

SUAV (Small UAV) Lightweight drones for photography or monitoring.

MAV (Micro Air Vehicle) Very small drones for research or indoor use.

docs.title: 4) Surface Robots (USV — Uncrewed Surface Vehicles)
docs.text: Surface robots operate on water surfaces.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Autonomous boats
  • Environmental monitoring vessels
  • Ocean data collection robots

docs.title: Why they are useful
docs.text: They can travel long distances on water without human crews.

docs.title: 5) Underwater Robots (UUV — Uncrewed Underwater Vehicles)
docs.text: These robots operate below the water surface.

docs.title: ROUV (Remotely Operated Underwater Vehicle)
docs.text: Controlled by humans through cables or wireless links.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Underwater inspection robots
  • Oil pipeline inspection robots

They are used where real-time human control is needed.

docs.title: AUV (Autonomous Underwater Vehicle)
docs.text: Operates without continuous human control.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Deep-sea exploration robots
  • Ocean mapping robots

They make decisions based on onboard sensors.

docs.title: 6) Space Robots
docs.text: Robots used in space missions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Mars rovers
  • Lunar robots
  • Robotic arms on the International Space Station

docs.title: Why they are useful
docs.text: They survive extreme temperatures, radiation, and vacuum.

docs.title: 7) Remote-Controlled Robots
docs.text:
These robots are directly controlled by humans.

They are not fully autonomous.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• RC cars
  • Teleoperated surgery robots
  • Remote inspection robots

They depend on human decisions but still perform physical tasks.

docs.title: Comparison of Different Types of Robots
docs.text: Type of Robot Where It Operates Control Type Examples Why It Is Used Ground Robots (UGV) Land Remote or Autonomous Warehouse robots, Mars rover, bomb disposal robot Carry loads, navigate terrain, work in hazardous areas Aerial Robots (UAV) Air Remote or Autonomous Delivery drones, surveillance drones, mapping drones Cover large areas quickly, reach high or risky places Surface Robots (USV) Water surface Mostly Autonomous Autonomous boats, monitoring vessels Long-duration water monitoring and data collection Underwater Robots (ROUV) Underwater Remotely Operated Pipeline inspection robots, underwater cameras Human-controlled exploration and inspection Underwater Robots (AUV) Underwater Autonomous Deep-sea exploration robots, ocean mapping robots Explore deep water without constant human control Space Robots Space Mostly Autonomous Mars rovers, ISS robotic arm Operate in extreme, human-unfriendly environments Remote-Controlled Robots Land/Water/Air Fully Human-Controlled RC cars, teleoperated surgery robots Human precision and decision-making in risky tasks

docs.title: Unmanned vs Uncrewed
docs.text:
Term Meaning Note Unmanned No human onboard Older term Uncrewed No human onboard Modern, gender-neutral term

Both refer to robots or vehicles operating without a person inside.

docs.title: Key Idea
docs.text:
Robots are often categorized by: - where they operate (land, air, water, space) - how they are controlled (remote vs autonomous)

Different environments require different robot designs.

docs.title: Self-Check Questions
docs.text:
1. Why is a chess AI not a robot?
  2. Give two examples of sensors.
  3. What are the 4 D’s?
  4. Why is a self-driving car high roboticity?

docs.title: Part A — MCQ (Choose ONE best answer)
Q1
docs.text:
Which system is MOST clearly a robot?

A) Chess AI on a laptop B) Voice assistant on a phone C) Robot vacuum navigating a room D) Weather prediction software

docs.title: Q2
docs.text:
A machine that senses and acts physically but always follows one fixed program with no change is:

A) High roboticity B) Medium roboticity C) Low roboticity D) Not a robot at all

docs.title: Q3
docs.text:
Which BEST explains why robots are used in bomb disposal?

A) Robots are cheaper B) Robots are more intelligent C) Robots reduce risk to humans D) Robots work faster

docs.title: Q4
docs.text:
Which example is AI but NOT a robot?

A) Self-driving car B) Robot dog C) Chess AI D) Delivery drone

docs.title: Q5
docs.text:
Which task is LEAST suitable for robots under the 4D rule?

A) Cleaning toxic waste B) Deep-sea exploration C) Creative storytelling for children D) Bomb disposal

docs.title: Q6
docs.text: A machine without a physical body can still be a robot if it is intelligent.

docs.title: Q7
docs.text: A remotely controlled robot is not considered a robot because it lacks autonomy.

docs.title: Q8
docs.text: A dishwasher may appear robotic but is usually considered low roboticity.

docs.title: Q9
docs.text: A robot must always look human-like to be considered a robot.

docs.title: Q10
docs.text: A robot that perfectly follows orders is always safe.

docs.title: Scenario 1 — The Fast Warehouse Robot
docs.text:
A company deploys mobile robots in a warehouse. They move very fast to improve efficiency.

Workers notice that robots sometimes pass very close to them. One worker almost gets hit while carrying items.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text: Q1) Which robotics principle is at risk here? Q2) Which of the 4D rules applies to warehouse work? Q3) What sensor improvement could reduce risk? Q4) Should robots prioritize speed or safety? Why?

docs.title: Scenario 2 — The “Do-Everything” Robot
docs.text:
A startup builds one robot that can: - cook food - clean rooms - teach children - drive a car

The robot becomes very expensive and unreliable.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text: Q1) Which robotics concept explains this failure? Q2) Why are task-specific robots usually better? Q3) Is this robot high or low practicality? Why? Q4) Give one example where specialization works better.

docs.title: Scenario 3 — The Smart but Bodiless AI
docs.text:
A company creates a very intelligent AI that: - plans schedules - gives medical suggestions - predicts traffic

It exists only as software.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text: Q1) Is this a robot? Why or why not? Q2) Is it AI? Why? Q3) What is missing for it to be a robot? Q4) If connected to a robot body, what changes?

docs.title: Scenario 4 — The Over-Obedient Robot
docs.text:
A home robot follows commands perfectly. A child jokingly tells it to push a chair toward someone.

The robot tries to follow the command.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text: Q1) Which Asimov law should stop this? Q2) What design feature could prevent harm? Q3) Why is blind obedience dangerous? Q4) Should robots question unsafe commands?

docs.title: Scenario 5 — The Deep-Sea Mission
docs.text:
Scientists send a robot deep underwater. Pressure is extreme and humans cannot survive there.

The robot collects data for hours.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text: Q1) Which “D” from the 4D rule applies most? Q2) Why are robots better than humans here? Q3) Is this robot remote or autonomous? Q4) What failure would be most dangerous in this environment?

docs.title: Scenario 6 — The Remote Drone
docs.text: A drone is controlled entirely by a human pilot. It has cameras and motors but no autonomy.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text: Q1) Is this still a robot? Why? Q2) What type of robot is it? Q3) Does low autonomy mean low roboticity? Q4) What would increase its roboticity?

docs.title: True/False
docs.text: 6) False 7) False 8) True 9) False 10) False

docs.title: Scenario 1 — The Fast Warehouse Robot
docs.text:
Q1) Which robotics principle is at risk here? Human safety and safe robot behavior are at risk.

Q2) Which of the 4D rules applies to warehouse work? Dull (repetitive box moving). Sometimes Dangerous if heavy loads are involved.

Q3) What sensor improvement could reduce risk? Better human detection using LIDAR, cameras, or proximity sensors.

Q4) Should robots prioritize speed or safety? Why? Safety. A robot that is fast but unsafe is not acceptable around humans.

docs.title: Scenario 2 — The “Do-Everything” Robot
docs.text:
Q1) Which robotics concept explains this failure? Application-specific design. Robots are more reliable when specialized.

Q2) Why are task-specific robots usually better? They are simpler, cheaper, and more reliable.

Q3) Is this robot high or low practicality? Why? Low practicality. Too complex and costly for real-world use.

Q4) Give one example where specialization works better. A robot vacuum designed only for cleaning floors.

docs.title: Scenario 3 — The Smart but Bodiless AI
docs.text:
Q1) Is this a robot? Why or why not? No. It has no physical body.

Q2) Is it AI? Why? Yes. It makes intelligent decisions and predictions.

Q3) What is missing for it to be a robot? A physical body with sensors and actuators.

Q4) If connected to a robot body, what changes? It becomes both AI and robotics.

docs.title: Scenario 4 — The Over-Obedient Robot
docs.text:
Q1) Which Asimov law should stop this? Law 1: A robot may not harm a human.

Q2) What design feature could prevent harm? Safety rules and collision avoidance.

Q3) Why is blind obedience dangerous? It can lead to harmful actions.

Q4) Should robots question unsafe commands? Yes. Safety should override obedience.

docs.title: Scenario 5 — The Deep-Sea Mission
docs.text:
Q1) Which “D” from the 4D rule applies most? Difficult.

Q2) Why are robots better than humans here? Humans cannot survive deep-sea pressure.

Q3) Is this robot remote or autonomous? It can be either, depending on design.

Q4) What failure would be most dangerous in this environment? Loss of communication or power.

docs.title: Scenario 6 — The Remote Drone
docs.text:
Q1) Is this still a robot? Why? Yes. It has a body, sensors, and actuators.

Q2) What type of robot is it? Remote-controlled robot (teleoperated).

Q3) Does low autonomy mean low roboticity? Not always. It can still be robotic but with lower autonomy.

Q4) What would increase its roboticity? Adding autonomy, decision-making, and adaptation.

docs.title: Robotics Primitives: Sense, Plan, Act, Learn
docs.text:
Robots operate using a small set of core abilities. These are called the primitives of robotics.

They describe how a robot interacts with the world and completes tasks.

The four main primitives are:

  • Sense
  • Plan
  • Act
  • Learn

Together, they form the basic intelligence loop of a robot.

docs.title: 1) Sense
docs.text:
Sensing is how a robot gathers information about the world.

A robot uses sensors to detect: - distance - light - sound - position - obstacles - people

Without sensing, a robot is blind to its environment.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Environment → Sensors → Robot

Example explanation:

A robot vacuum uses: - distance sensors to detect walls - bump sensors to detect collisions - cameras or LIDAR to understand layout

If sensing fails, the robot cannot make good decisions.

docs.title: 2) Plan
docs.text:
Planning is deciding what to do next based on sensed information.

The robot: - interprets sensor data - chooses a goal - decides a sequence of actions

Planning answers: "What should I do now?"

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Start → Path → Goal

Example explanation:

A delivery robot plans: - shortest path to destination - how to avoid obstacles - when to turn or stop

Planning can be simple or very complex depending on the task.

docs.title: 3) Act
docs.text:
Acting is when the robot physically does something.

Actions are executed through: - motors - wheels - arms - grippers

Acting changes the real world.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Decision → Motor Command → Movement

Example explanation:

A robot arm receives command: "Move to position X"

Motors rotate → arm moves → object is picked.

Without action, sensing and planning have no effect.

docs.title: 4) Learn
docs.text:
Learning allows a robot to improve over time.

A learning robot: - remembers past experiences - adjusts behavior - improves performance

Learning is common in AI-based robots.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Example explanation:

A robot vacuum learns: - which areas are usually dirty - which paths are faster - where obstacles often appear

Over time, it becomes more efficient.

docs.title: Putting It Together
docs.text:
A robot continuously loops:

Sense → Plan → Act → (Learn) → Sense again

This loop runs many times per second in real robots.

docs.title: Key Idea
docs.text:
All robots, from simple to advanced, rely on these primitives.

More advanced robots: - sense better - plan smarter - act more precisely - learn faster

docs.title: What is a Paradigm?
docs.text:
Before learning different robot control styles, we must understand one important word:

Paradigm.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A paradigm is a set of ideas, methods, and assumptions that guide how problems are understood and solved.

It is like a "way of thinking" or a framework.

A paradigm influences: - how we design systems - how we solve problems - what we believe is important

When a paradigm changes, the way we build systems also changes.

docs.title: Simple Meaning
docs.text:
A paradigm is: "How you think about a problem before solving it."

Different paradigms lead to different solutions for the same problem.

docs.title: Example (Everyday Life)
docs.text:
Write on board:

Problem: Go to university

Two people may use different paradigms:

Person A: Plans full route → checks map → follows plan strictly

Person B: Just starts walking → reacts to traffic and obstacles

Both reach the destination, but their thinking style is different.

These thinking styles are like paradigms.

docs.title: Science Example
docs.text:
In science, paradigms change how we understand reality.

Example:

Newtonian Mechanics - World is predictable - Physics is deterministic

Quantum Mechanics - World is probabilistic - Outcomes are uncertain

Both explain the world, but in very different ways.

When the paradigm changed, scientists built new models and tools.

docs.title: Robotics Connection
docs.text:
In robotics, a paradigm decides:

  • How the robot thinks
  • How it makes decisions
  • How it uses sensor data
  • How it controls actions

Different robotics paradigms lead to very different robot designs.

docs.title: Why Paradigms Matter in Robotics
docs.text:
If you believe: "The robot must plan everything first" → you build a planning-heavy robot

If you believe: "The robot should react instantly" → you build a reactive robot

So the paradigm shapes the robot’s behavior.

docs.title: Key Idea
docs.text:
A paradigm is not right or wrong. It is a design philosophy.

Different paradigms work better for different situations.

In the next parts, we will study major robotics paradigms.

docs.title: Hierarchical / Deliberative Paradigm
docs.text:
Now that we understand what a paradigm is, the next question is:

How should a robot make decisions?

Should it: - think carefully first, then act? OR - act immediately based on sensors?

Early robotics researchers believed:

"A robot should think before acting."

This idea led to the Hierarchical (Deliberative) Paradigm.

docs.title: Core Idea
docs.text:
Think first, act later.

The robot: 1) builds a model of the world 2) plans what to do 3) executes the plan

Sense → Plan → Act

Planning is the most important step.

docs.title: Why It Is Called Hierarchical
docs.text:
It is hierarchical because decisions are layered:

High level: - Goals - Missions - Long-term planning

Low level: - Movements - Motor commands

The top level controls the lower levels.

docs.title: World Model Concept
docs.text:
The robot maintains a global world model.

This is an internal map or representation of the environment.

Example: - map of a building - positions of obstacles - known locations

The robot thinks using this model before making a move.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Sense → Build Map → Plan Path → Act

Example explanation:

A robot wants to go to an office.

Step 1: It scans environment and builds a map.

Step 2: It calculates the best route.

Step 3: It moves according to the plan.

It trusts its plan.

docs.title: STRIPS Idea (Simple View)
docs.text:
Early planning systems assumed: - the world is predictable - the model is correct - nothing unexpected happens

This is called a closed-world assumption.

Meaning: "If it is not in the model, it does not exist."

docs.title: Strengths
docs.text:
• Logical and structured
  • Good for known environments
  • Clear decision-making process
  • Works well when world is stable

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
Real world is messy.

Problems: - planning takes time - world changes unexpectedly - sensor errors break plans

Example: Robot plans path → chair moves → plan fails.

The robot must re-plan again and again.

This makes it slow.

docs.title: Why Some People Disliked It
docs.text:
Users: - too slow in real environments

Control engineers: - not closed-loop enough

AI researchers: - too monolithic and rigid

docs.title: Key Idea
docs.text:
Hierarchical paradigm assumes: "If the robot thinks enough, it will act correctly."

But real environments are dynamic.

This leads to a big question:

What if the robot stops planning so much and just reacts?

That question leads to the next paradigm.

docs.title: Reactive Paradigm
docs.text:
We just saw that the hierarchical paradigm plans a lot before acting.

But real environments change quickly.

People noticed: - robots were too slow - plans became outdated - unexpected obstacles broke plans

So researchers asked:

"What if robots stop overthinking and simply react to the world?"

This idea led to the Reactive Paradigm.

docs.title: Core Idea
docs.text:
The world is its own best model.

Instead of building a big internal map, the robot directly reacts to sensor inputs.

Sense → Act

No heavy planning step.

docs.title: Key Principle
docs.text:
Direct connection between perception and action.

Sensors trigger actions immediately.

Example: If obstacle detected → turn If path clear → move forward

No long-term thinking required.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Sensor Input → Immediate Action

Example explanation:

A wall-following robot:

Wall appears → sensor detects → robot turns Path clears → robot moves forward Another object appears → robot turns again

The robot only looks at current sensor values.

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text:
• No global map
  • No long-term memory
  • No complex planning
  • Tight coupling of sensing and action
  • Focus on real-time response

Each behavior works independently.

docs.title: Biological Inspiration
docs.text:
Many animals behave this way.

Example: An insect avoids obstacles without building a map of the world.

Reactive robotics takes inspiration from such biological systems.

docs.title: Strengths
docs.text:
• Very fast responses
  • Works well in dynamic environments
  • Simple to implement
  • Robust to sudden changes

Robots do not waste time planning.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
No big-picture thinking.

Problems include: - local minima (getting stuck) - wandering without direction - no memory of past mistakes

Example: Robot stuck in a corner keeps turning randomly.

Sometimes random motion is used to escape traps.

docs.title: Why People Reacted to It
docs.text:
Users: - liked it because it worked in real time

AI researchers: - liked it but wanted planning back

Control engineers: - disliked lack of formal guarantees

docs.title: Key Idea
docs.text:
Reactive paradigm assumes: "Fast reaction is better than deep planning."

But now another question appears:

What if we want both? - global planning AND - fast reactions?

That leads to the next paradigm.

docs.title: Hybrid Deliberative / Reactive Paradigm
docs.text:
We have seen two extremes:

Hierarchical paradigm: - smart planning - but slow and fragile in dynamic worlds

Reactive paradigm: - fast and robust - but lacks long-term direction

So researchers asked:

"Why not combine both?"

Use planning for direction, and reactions for safety.

This idea led to the Hybrid Paradigm.

docs.title: Core Idea
docs.text:
Think globally, act locally.

The robot: - plans at a high level - reacts at a low level

Both systems work together.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Two main layers:

1) Planning Layer (Deliberative) - builds maps - sets goals - computes paths - decides where to go

Answers: "Where should I go?"

2) Reactive Layer - reads sensors continuously - avoids obstacles - handles surprises - ensures safety

Answers: "What should I do right now?"

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Planner → Goal Direction Reactive → Immediate Safety

Example explanation:

Task: Go from lab to office.

Planner: Lab → corridor → stairs → office

While moving: A chair appears

Reactive layer: Turn immediately to avoid

After avoidance: Control returns to planner

Robot continues toward office.

docs.title: Simple Rule
docs.text:
Planner gives purpose. Reactive layer ensures survival.

One thinks long-term. One acts short-term.

docs.title: Local vs Global Models
docs.text:
Hybrid systems use both:

Global model: - maps - mission goals - long-term route

Local model: - current obstacles - nearby people - immediate surroundings

Both are necessary for good performance.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Practical in real environments
  • Balances intelligence and speed
  • Modular design
  • Asynchronous processing

Planner can compute next goals while robot reacts to obstacles.

docs.title: Why People Liked It
docs.text:
Users: - liked it because it worked reliably

AI researchers: - liked the planning component

Control engineers: - accepted it due to closed-loop behavior

It satisfied many groups.

docs.title: Key Idea
docs.text:
Hybrid paradigm assumes:

"Plan for direction, react for safety."

This is how many modern robots operate today.

docs.title: Local vs Global Models in Robotics
docs.text:
In the hybrid paradigm we said:

  • Planner thinks globally
  • Reactive layer acts locally

But what does "local" and "global" actually mean?

Why does a robot need both?

To answer this, we discuss local and global models.

docs.title: Global Model
docs.text:
A global model is the robot’s big-picture understanding of the world.

It includes: - maps - known locations - mission goals - planned routes

It helps the robot decide long-term direction.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Write:

Global Model = Map + Goal + Route

Example:

A robot knows: - where the lab is - where the office is - which corridor connects them

So it plans: Lab → Corridor → Office

This is global thinking.

docs.title: Local Model
docs.text:
A local model is the robot’s immediate understanding of its surroundings.

It includes: - nearby obstacles - moving people - sudden changes - current sensor readings

It helps the robot act safely right now.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Local Model = Current Sensors

Example:

While moving to office: A person walks in front.

Local model detects person → robot slows down or turns.

This is local control.

docs.title: Why Global Alone Is Not Enough
docs.text:
If robot only uses global model: - it may ignore sudden obstacles - it may collide with people - map may be outdated

Global planning assumes the world stays the same.

But real world changes.

docs.title: Why Local Alone Is Not Enough
docs.text:
If robot only reacts locally: - it has no long-term goal - it may wander randomly - it may never reach destination

Reactive robots survive but may not achieve missions.

docs.title: Balanced Approach
docs.text:
Good robots combine both.

Global model: - decides where to go

Local model: - decides how to move safely

Together they provide: - direction - safety - adaptability

docs.title: Key Idea
docs.text:
Global = Purpose Local = Safety

A successful robot needs both to perform well in real environments.

docs.title: How Robots Work: Robot Subsystems
docs.text:
So far we discussed: - how robots think (paradigms) - how they plan and react - how they use local and global models

Now a practical question:

What actually makes a robot work?

A robot is not just intelligence. It is a combination of subsystems working together.

docs.title: Core Robot Subsystems
docs.text:
A robot typically has:

  • Sense (Perception/Recognition)
  • Plan (Control/Decision)
  • Act (Motion/Manipulation)
  • Power
  • Communication

Each subsystem has a role.

docs.title: 1) Sense (Perception)
docs.text:
This subsystem gathers information from the environment.

It answers: "What is happening around me?"

Examples: - camera - LIDAR - ultrasonic sensors - GPS - IMU

Without sensing: The robot is blind.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
World → Sensors → Robot

Example explanation:

A robot vacuum detects: - walls - furniture - stairs

This data allows safe movement.

docs.title: 2) Plan (Control/Decision)
docs.text:
This subsystem processes information and decides actions.

It answers: "What should I do next?"

Examples: - path planning - obstacle avoidance decisions - task scheduling

Planning turns data into decisions.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Sensor Data → Decision → Command

Example:

If obstacle detected → decide to turn.

docs.title: 3) Act (Motion/Manipulation)
docs.text:
This subsystem executes actions in the real world.

Examples: - wheels moving - robotic arms lifting - grippers holding objects

It answers: "How do I perform the action?"

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Command → Motors → Movement

Example:

Robot arm receives command → motors rotate → object is picked.

docs.title: 4) Power
docs.text:
Robots need energy to operate.

Examples: - batteries - wired power supply - solar power

Without power: Nothing works.

Power limits: - operation time - motor strength - computation ability

docs.title: 5) Communication
docs.text:
Allows robots to send and receive data.

Examples: - Wi-Fi - Bluetooth - radio signals - wired networks

Used for: - remote control - cloud processing - multi-robot coordination

docs.title: Putting It All Together
docs.text:
All subsystems work in a loop:

Sense → Plan → Act ↑ ↓ Power & Communication support all

If one subsystem fails, robot performance drops.

docs.title: Key Idea
docs.text:
A robot is a system-of-systems.

Good robotics requires: - good sensors - smart planning - reliable actuation - stable power - effective communication

docs.title: Sensors in Robotics
docs.text:
We said robots must sense the world.

But how do they actually do that?

Robots cannot see, hear, or feel like humans. They rely on sensors.

Sensors are the robot’s connection to the real world.

Without sensors: - no awareness - no safe navigation - no intelligent behavior

docs.title: What is a Sensor?
docs.text:
A sensor is a device that detects physical properties of the environment and converts them into signals a robot can process.

Sensors measure things like: - distance - light - temperature - motion - position

docs.title: Active vs Passive Sensors
docs.text: This is a key classification.

docs.title: Active Sensors
docs.text:
Active sensors send out energy and measure the response.

They emit signals like: - sound waves - infrared light - laser pulses

Then they measure the reflection.

docs.title: Example Logic
docs.text: Send signal → hit object → return signal → compute distance

docs.title: Why They Are Useful
docs.text:
• Work in darkness
  • Give direct distance info
  • Less dependent on lighting

docs.title: Why They Are Not Always Ideal
docs.text:
• Consume more power
  • Can be affected by interference
  • Sometimes limited range

docs.title: Passive Sensors
docs.text:
Passive sensors do NOT emit energy. They only detect energy from environment.

Examples: - cameras - microphones - light sensors

docs.title: Why They Are Useful
docs.text:
• Low power consumption
  • Rich environmental information
  • Natural sensing

docs.title: Why They Are Not Always Ideal
docs.text:
• Depend on lighting or conditions
  • Harder to estimate distance directly
  • Sensitive to noise

docs.title: 1) Ultrasonic Sensor
docs.text: Type: Active

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
• Sends ultrasonic sound waves
  • Measures echo return time
  • Calculates distance

docs.title: Example
docs.text: Send sound → Echo returns → Distance

docs.title: Good Because
docs.text:
• Cheap
  • Simple
  • Works in dark
  • Good for obstacle detection

docs.title: Not Ideal Because
docs.text:
• Low resolution
  • Wide beam (less precise)
  • Soft materials absorb sound

Example issue: Curtains may not reflect well.

docs.title: 2) Infrared (IR) Sensor
docs.text: Type: Active (usually)

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
• Emits infrared light
  • Measures reflected light

docs.title: Good Because
docs.text:
• Small and low-cost
  • Good for short distances
  • Fast response

Used in: - line-following robots - proximity detection

docs.title: Not Ideal Because
docs.text:
• Sensitive to sunlight
  • Affected by surface color
  • Limited range

Example issue: Black surfaces absorb IR.

docs.title: 3) LiDAR
docs.text: Type: Active

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
• Sends laser pulses
  • Measures return time
  • Builds precise distance map

docs.title: Example
docs.text: Laser pulse → Reflection → 3D Map

docs.title: Good Because
docs.text:
• Very accurate
  • High resolution
  • Creates maps
  • Great for navigation

Used in: - self-driving cars - mapping robots - SLAM systems

docs.title: Not Ideal Because
docs.text:
• Expensive
  • Higher power use
  • Can struggle in rain/fog

docs.title: Quick Comparison
docs.text: Sensor Accuracy Cost Range Notes Ultrasonic Medium Low Medium Simple obstacle detection IR Low-Medium Very Low Short Sensitive to surfaces LiDAR Very High High Long Mapping and navigation

docs.title: Summary of Sensors
docs.text:
Sensors are critical because they: - provide environmental awareness - enable safe movement - support planning and control

No single sensor is perfect.

Good robots often use: multiple sensors together (sensor fusion)

Example: Camera + LiDAR + IMU → more reliable perception

docs.title: Key Idea
docs.text:
Better sensing leads to: - better decisions - safer robots - smarter behavior

A robot is only as good as the information it receives.

docs.title: Part A — MCQ (Choose ONE best answer)
Q1
docs.text:
Which sequence best represents the core robotics loop?

A) Plan → Sense → Act B) Sense → Plan → Act C) Act → Sense → Plan D) Sense → Act → Forget

docs.title: Q2
docs.text:
Which paradigm relies MOST on a global world model?

A) Reactive B) Hybrid C) Hierarchical/Deliberative D) Behavior-based

docs.title: Q3
docs.text:
A robot that turns immediately when a sensor detects a wall is using:

A) Deliberative control B) Reactive control C) Hybrid planning D) Global modeling

docs.title: Q4
docs.text:
Which is a passive sensor?

A) LiDAR B) Ultrasonic C) Camera D) IR proximity sensor

docs.title: Q5
docs.text:
Why is LiDAR widely used in navigation?

A) Cheapest sensor B) Needs no power C) High accuracy mapping D) Works only indoors

docs.title: Q6
docs.text: Reactive robots do not need any sensors.

docs.title: Q7
docs.text: Hierarchical robots assume their world model is correct.

docs.title: Q8
docs.text: Local models focus on immediate surroundings.

docs.title: Q9
docs.text: A robot without learning cannot be intelligent.

docs.title: Q10
docs.text: Active sensors emit energy to measure the environment.

docs.title: MCQ
docs.text:
Q1 — B Robotics loop is Sense → Plan → Act.

Q2 — C Hierarchical relies on global models.

Q3 — B Immediate reaction = reactive control.

Q4 — C Camera is passive (no emission).

Q5 — C LiDAR is used for accurate mapping.

docs.title: True/False
docs.text:
Q6 — False Reactive robots rely heavily on sensors.

Q7 — True Deliberative assumes model correctness.

Q8 — True Local = immediate surroundings.

Q9 — False Learning is optional in many robots.

Q10 — True Active sensors emit energy.

docs.title: Scenario 1 — The “Smart” Tour Guide Robot
docs.text: A museum robot: - has a full map of the building - plans routes between exhibits - BUT if a child steps in front, it immediately stops or turns

docs.title: Question
docs.text:
Which paradigm BEST describes this robot?

A) Reactive B) Hierarchical/Deliberative C) Hybrid

docs.title: Correct Answer
docs.text: C) Hybrid

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
• Uses global map → deliberative component
  • Reacts instantly to people → reactive component
  • Combines planning + reaction

docs.title: Why NOT Others
docs.text:
Reactive: - No map or planning

Hierarchical: - Would stop and re-plan fully instead of quick avoidance

docs.title: Scenario 2 — The Overconfident Planner
docs.text: A robot in a warehouse: - builds a perfect map - computes full path - follows it strictly even when obstacles appear - frequently stops to re-plan

docs.title: Question
docs.text:
Which paradigm is this?

A) Reactive B) Hierarchical C) Hybrid

docs.title: Why

• Heavy reliance on planning
  • Strong world model
  • Stops to re-plan

docs.title: Why NOT Others
docs.text:
Reactive: - Would not build map

Hybrid: - Would avoid locally without constant re-planning

docs.title: Question
docs.text:
Which paradigm?

A) Reactive B) Hierarchical C) Hybrid

docs.text:

docs.text: A small robot: - must save power - only needs general scene understanding - operates in well-lit area

docs.text:
Best sensor?

docs.title: Why NOT Others

docs.text: A drone: - plans route using GPS - avoids birds instantly using sensors - resumes route after avoidance

docs.title: Question
docs.text:
Which paradigm?

A) Reactive B) Hierarchical C) Hybrid

docs.title: Correct Answer
docs.text: C) Hybrid

docs.title: Why NOT Others
